d: Explains how to schedule code so it executes after a specific action or cycle has completed.
h:
Scheduling code is useful in many situations, such as ensuring code executes after a specific action or cycle has completed, or delaying code for a specific duration of time. You can use the task library to optimize Roblox's task scheduler to manage and schedule code. You can also use a similar library called coroutine to schedule code which has some additional functionality.

Common methods

The following are the most common task methods used to schedule code. You should use the task methods over legacy scheduling methods, such as RobloxGlobals.wait(), to ensure that your code runs optimally.

Certain legacy global methods, such as (RobloxGlobals.spawn(), RobloxGlobals.delay(), and RobloxGlobals.wait()) can provide similar code scheduling results but are less optimized and configurable as their task alternatives. If your game uses these legacy methods, you should use task instead to ensure your game's code remains efficient and up-to-date.

The following table lists the relevant legacy global methods and their preferred, more optimized counterparts:

Legacy global methods Task methods Additional alternatives
wait() task.wait() RunService.Heartbeat
wait(n) task.wait(n)
spawn(f) task.defer(f) task.delay(0, f)
delay(n, f) task.delay(n, f)
spawn(function() f(uv1, ...) end) task.defer(f, uv1, ...) task.delay(0, f, uv1, ...)
delay(n, function() f(uv1, ...) end) task.delay(n, f, uv1, ...)

task.spawn()

task.spawn() takes a thread or function and resumes it immediately through the engine's scheduler. Additional arguments are passed to the thread or function being resumed.

The following code sample is an example of how you can use task.spawn() when calling a function that may yield while iterating over a set of objects:

local function playerAdded(player)
    print(player)
end

for _, player in Players:GetPlayers() do
    task.spawn(playerAdded, player)
end

task.defer()

task.defer() takes a thread or function and defers it until the end of the current resume point within the current frame. Additional arguments are passed to the thread or function resuming.

You should typically use this when you want similar behavior to task.spawn() but don't care about the thread running immediately. The following code sample illustrates how the RobloxGlobals.print() statement for "A" will defer until after the RobloxGlobals.print() statement for "B" executes:

task.defer(print, "A")
print("B")
--> B
--> A

task.defer() is an optimized version of RobloxGlobals.spawn() that schedules a thread to resume as soon as possible (but not immediately) without any throttling.

task.delay()

task.delay() takes a thread or function and schedules it for resumption after the given amount of time elapses on the next Heartbeat step. The thread resumes with built-in error handling and support for other engine features. Any additional arguments are passed to the thread or function resuming.

Since the actual delay time may vary, the following code sample illustrates how you can calculate it by passing the current time as an argument:

task.delay(2, function(scheduledTime)
    print(os.clock() - scheduledTime) --> 2.038702
end, os.clock())

A duration of zero will result in the thread or function resuming on the next step.

task.delay() is an optimized version of RobloxGlobals.delay() that schedules a thread to resume after some time elapses without throttling.

task.wait()

task.wait() yields the current thread until the given duration (in seconds) elapses and then resumes the thread on the next Heartbeat step.

The actual yield time may vary. The following code sample illustrates how this method returns it for convenience:

Since the actual delay time may vary, the following code sample illustrates how you can get the actual time by storing the method's return value:

local elapsedTime = task.wait(2) -- Wait for 2 seconds
print(elapsedTime) --> 2.0792941

If no duration is given the duration will default to zero meaning the thread will automatically resume on the next step. This means task.wait() is equivalent in behavior to RunService.Heartbeat.

task.wait() is an optimized version of RobloxGlobals.wait() that schedules the current thread to resume after some time elapses without throttling.

kid.simple: This page is about deciding when your code runs. Sometimes you want code to wait a few seconds, run a little later, or run right now without blocking the rest of the script. The `task` library gives you simple tools for all of these. Using them keeps your game smooth and your code up to date.
kid.analogy: Think of a teacher handing out jobs. `task.spawn` means "do this right now", `task.defer` means "do this as soon as I finish talking", `task.delay` means "do this in 5 minutes", and `task.wait` means "everyone pause for 5 minutes".
keyPoints: The `task` library is the modern way to schedule code in Roblox.
Old global functions like `wait()`, `spawn()`, and `delay()` still work but are slower and less flexible, so use `task.wait()`, `task.defer()`, and `task.delay()` instead.
`task.spawn(f, ...)` starts a function right away, so a slow function will not hold up the rest of your loop.
`task.defer(f, ...)` runs a function a tiny bit later, after the current code finishes, but still in the same frame.
`task.delay(seconds, f, ...)` runs a function after a number of seconds.
`task.wait(seconds)` pauses the current script, then gives back how long it really waited.
Real wait times are never exact. `task.wait(2)` might really take about 2.08 seconds.
`task.wait()` with no number waits just one step, like waiting for the next `Heartbeat`.

terms.schedule: To set up code so it runs at a certain time, like later or after something else finishes.
terms.thread: One line of work your script is doing. Roblox can keep many threads going and switch between them.
terms.yield: To pause. A function that yields stops and waits (for example for 2 seconds) before it keeps going.
terms.resume: To un-pause a thread so it keeps running from where it stopped.
terms.frame: One tiny slice of game time. Roblox runs about 60 frames every second.
terms.Heartbeat: An event from `RunService` that fires once every frame, after physics is done. `task.wait` and `task.delay` resume on the next Heartbeat.
terms.defer: To put something off until a little later. `task.defer` runs your function after the code that is running right now is done.
terms.legacy: Old. Legacy methods like `wait()` still work but newer ones are better.
terms.task scheduler: The part of the Roblox engine that decides what work happens in each frame and in what order.
terms.throttling: Slowing things down on purpose. The old `wait()` could be slowed down by the engine; `task.wait()` is not.

example.title: Countdown and a delayed message
example.code:
-- Count down from 3, then announce a start after a short delay
for i = 3, 1, -1 do
	print(i)
	task.wait(1) -- pause this script for about 1 second
end

-- Run a function 2 seconds from now, without pausing this script
task.delay(2, function()
	print("Bonus round starts now!")
end)

-- Run a function right away in its own thread
task.spawn(function()
	print("Go!")
end)

print("This prints before the bonus message")
explain: The `for` loop prints 3, 2, 1 and uses `task.wait(1)` to pause about one second between numbers.
`task.delay(2, ...)` sets up a function to run in about 2 seconds. The script does not stop to wait for it.
`task.spawn` runs its function right now, so "Go!" prints immediately.
The last `print` runs before the bonus message, because `task.delay` did not pause the script.

watchOut: Using old `wait()`, `spawn()`, or `delay()`. Swap them for `task.wait()`, `task.defer()`, and `task.delay()`.
Expecting exact timing. `task.wait(2)` waits at least 2 seconds, usually a little more. Use the number it returns if you need the real time.
Putting a slow function in a loop and wondering why the loop is slow. Wrap the call in `task.spawn` so each one starts right away.
Thinking `task.defer` runs instantly. It runs after the current code finishes, so its print may come after lines written below it.
